Variants.Content: Joachim of Fiore died in 1202, but his writings continue to circulate in 1259. Readers interpret his division of history into ages in different ways, and some followers associate the coming year 1260 with an approaching spiritual transformation. Reports of Mongol campaigns in the east and local illness or unusual weather can intensify such fears, but they do not prove that the end is near. Preachers may criticise clerical wealth or call for apostolic poverty; bishops and abbots respond according to local circumstances. A courtier can worry that radical interpretations challenge church authority, yet should distinguish an expectation from a fulfilled prophecy. The year ahead is a focus of speculation, not a known turning point.

A scholar or friar in 1259 encounters Joachimite readings and debates whether 1260 marks a new age. Some Franciscans stress poverty; others reject attempts to calculate divine history. Bishops monitor arguments that may challenge authority, but Flagellant processions have not begun. Teachers attribute predictions to their proponents and note disagreement.

A preacher's expectation of a turning point around 1260 can unsettle a household already living with war and scarcity. Some listeners seek confession or give alms; others doubt the prediction. In 1259 no one can speak as a witness to next year's flagellant processions. Prophecy belongs to the speaker's belief and must remain distinct from a certain future event.
